title: Warden Academy PNG
disclaimer: This course is a training aid on the functions of a Mining Warden under the Mining Act 1992 (Papua New Guinea). Section numbers follow the Act as originally published (No. 20 of 1992, PacLII). Later amendments, including the Mineral Resources Authority Act and the Mining (Amendment) Act 2015, changed some office names (the 'Director' is now the Managing Director of the MRA and the 'Board' is now the Mining Advisory Council) and may have changed some section numbers. Always check the current consolidated Act and MRA guidance before you rely on a provision. This app is not legal advice.

modules.title: Foundations: The Act and the Office of Warden
modules.summary: Why the Mining Act exists, the types of tenement it creates, the people who administer it, and how Wardens are appointed.
objectives: Explain the purpose of the Mining Act 1992
Name the main types of tenement
Identify the key office holders and what each does
Describe how the Chief Warden and Wardens are appointed and how power is delegated

lessons.heading: Purpose of the Act
lessons.body: The Mining Act 1992 regulates the law on minerals and mining in Papua New Guinea. It sets up a licensing system so that exploration and mining happen in an orderly way and in the national interest, while the rights of landholders are respected through hearings and compensation.
bullets: Minerals are regulated by the State through tenements (licences and leases)
Landholders take part through Warden's hearings and compensation
The Act is administered today by the Mineral Resources Authority (MRA)

lessons.heading: Types of tenement
lessons.body: A 'tenement' is the general word for the rights the Act grants. A Warden deals with applications for all of them.
bullets: Exploration Licence (EL): to search for minerals
Mining Lease (ML): for medium-scale mining
Special Mining Lease (SML): for large-scale mining projects
Alluvial Mining Lease (AML): for small-scale alluvial mining, often by landholders
Lease for Mining Purposes (LMP): for infrastructure that supports mining
Mining Easement (ME): for access such as roads, pipelines and power lines

lessons.heading: Who's who
lessons.body: Several offices work together on every application. Knowing where the Warden sits stops you from overstepping your role.
bullets: Minister: grants or refuses most tenements, on recommendation
Managing Director of MRA (the 'Director' in the 1992 text): appoints Wardens
Registrar of Tenements: registers applications, fixes dates with the Chief Warden, publishes notices
Mining Advisory Council (the 'Board' in the 1992 text): considers reports and recommends to the Minister
Chief Warden: leads the Wardens, schedules hearings, handles compensation matters
Warden: conducts hearings, reports, determines compensation disputes

lessons.heading: Appointment, functions and delegation
lessons.body: Section 16 creates the office of Warden.
bullets: s 16(1): the Director appoints a Chief Warden from among officers, and other officers he considers necessary as Wardens
s 16(2): the functions, powers and duties of a Warden are as specified in the Act
s 16(3): the Chief Warden performs a Warden's duties plus any functions the Act gives specifically to the Chief Warden, or the Director refers to him
s 16(4): the Chief Warden may delegate in writing all or any of his powers to a Warden, except the power of delegation itself
lessons.note: A Warden has only the powers the Act gives. If the Act does not give a power, the Warden does not have it.

keyPoints: Wardens are statutory office holders appointed under s 16
A Warden's powers come only from the Act
The Chief Warden can delegate any power except the power to delegate
A Warden hears and reports. The Minister decides on the tenement.
modules.tokPisin: Warden em i ofisa we Managing Director bilong MRA i makim aninit long Section 16 bilong Mining Act 1992. Warden i ken mekim tasol ol wok we Act i tok long en.

quiz.prompt: Under s 16(1), who appoints the Chief Warden and the Wardens?
options: The Director (now the MRA Managing Director)
quiz.explanation: Section 16(1) says the Director appoints the Chief Warden and other Wardens from among officers. Today that is the Managing Director of the MRA.

quiz.prompt: Where are the functions, powers and duties of a Warden set out?
options: In the Warden's letter of appointment only
quiz.explanation: Section 16(2) says the functions, powers and duties of a Warden are as specified in the Act.

quiz.prompt: Which power can the Chief Warden NOT delegate to a Warden?
quiz.explanation: Under s 16(4), the Chief Warden may delegate all or any of his powers by written instrument, except the power of delegation itself.

quiz.prompt: A delegation from the Chief Warden to a Warden must be made…
options: By order of the National Court
quiz.explanation: Section 16(4) requires delegation by instrument in writing.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT a tenement under the Mining Act 1992?
quiz.explanation: Petroleum is regulated under separate oil and gas legislation. ELs, AMLs and Mining Easements are all tenements under the Mining Act.

quiz.prompt: Who makes the final decision to grant most tenements?
options: The Warden at the end of the hearing
quiz.explanation: The Warden hears and reports. The Mining Advisory Council recommends, and the Minister decides. The Warden does not grant tenements.

modules.title: Applications, Notice and Objections
modules.summary: What happens between lodging an application and the Warden's hearing: scheduling, publicity and objections.
objectives: State the timelines the Registrar must follow when scheduling a hearing
List how an application is publicised
Explain who may object and what happens to an objection

lessons.heading: Scheduling the hearing
lessons.body: Within seven days of registering an application, the Registrar must confer with the Chief Warden. Together they set the timetable.
bullets: The objection deadline must be at least 30 days after registration
Hearing dates and places are fixed 7 to 14 days after the objection deadline
The Registrar endorses the dates on the application and notifies the applicant in writing
lessons.note: The Chief Warden's input matters. Pick venues that affected landholders can actually reach, and leave Wardens enough travel time.

lessons.heading: Publicising the application
lessons.body: People can only object or attend if they know about the application. The Registrar must publicise it widely.
bullets: Send a copy to the relevant provincial government(s)
Publish it in the National Gazette
Send it to certain existing tenement holders, where relevant
Send it to nearby District and Sub-District Offices
Advertise it in a national newspaper
Keep it posted at headquarters until the application is determined

lessons.heading: Objections
lessons.body: Any person may lodge a written objection before the deadline fixed under s 105.
bullets: The objection must be in writing and lodged with the Registrar
The Registrar gives copies to the applicant and to the Executive Officer of the Board (Council)
The objection is kept posted at headquarters
lessons.note: Before the hearing, the Warden should read every objection so that each objector's concerns can be properly heard.

keyPoints: Registrar confers with the Chief Warden within 7 days of registration
The objection period is at least 30 days
The hearing is held 7 to 14 days after the objection deadline
Any person may object in writing
modules.tokPisin: Olgeta man i ken raitim pas bilong sakim (objection) aplikesen. Ol i mas givim pas long Registrar bipo long de laspela we Act i makim.

quiz.prompt: Within how many days of registering an application must the Registrar confer with the Chief Warden?
quiz.explanation: Section 105 requires the Registrar to confer with the Chief Warden within seven days of registration.

quiz.prompt: The last date for objections must be at least how long after registration?
quiz.explanation: The objection deadline must be at least 30 days after the application is registered.

quiz.prompt: When is the Warden's hearing held?
options: On the same day as the objection deadline
7 to 14 days after the objection deadline
quiz.explanation: Hearing dates and places are fixed 7 to 14 days after the last date for objections.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the s 106 publicity steps?
options: Sending to District and Sub-District Offices
quiz.explanation: Section 106 covers the provincial government, the Gazette, relevant tenement holders, District/Sub-District Offices, a national newspaper and posting at headquarters. Television is not listed.

quiz.prompt: Who may lodge an objection to an application?
quiz.explanation: Section 107 allows any person to lodge a written objection before the deadline.

quiz.prompt: Once an objection is lodged, the Registrar must give copies to…
options: The Minister and the Prime Minister
The applicant and the Board's Executive Officer
The police and the provincial administrator
quiz.explanation: The Registrar gives copies to the applicant and the Executive Officer of the Board (now the Mining Advisory Council), and keeps the objection posted at headquarters.

modules.title: Conducting the Warden's Hearing
modules.summary: The Warden's core function: running a fair hearing where the applicant explains the proposal and affected people are heard.
objectives: List the steps a Warden must take at a hearing under s 108
Explain the purpose of confirming identity and affected status
Know when and how a hearing may be adjourned
Use good-practice techniques for community hearings

lessons.heading: The statutory duties at a hearing
lessons.body: The Warden must attend the places and dates fixed and conduct a hearing that gives a fair opportunity to be heard to the applicant, the landholders and other persons affected.
bullets: Attend at the fixed places and dates
Give a fair opportunity to the applicant, landholders and others affected
Confirm the identity of those present and that they are affected by the proposal
Allow the applicant to explain the exploration programme or mining proposals
Record and assess the views of landholders and other affected persons

lessons.heading: Adjournment
lessons.body: The Warden may adjourn a hearing from time to time and from place to place, on whatever conditions the Warden sets, including conditions about costs.
bullets: Adjourn if key landholders could not attend because of weather, transport or a clash with a funeral or other custom
Adjourn if the applicant cannot properly explain its proposal
You may move the hearing to another village if more affected people can attend there
You may make the party that caused the adjournment pay the costs

lessons.heading: Why the hearing matters in PNG
lessons.body: Most land in PNG is customary land. MRA describes the hearing as essential, because it is how access to the land is negotiated for the tenement under application. A poorly run hearing can later invalidate a Ministerial decision.
bullets: The National Court has quashed a decision where the required hearing steps were not followed (PGNC 212 of 2013)
A fair hearing reduces conflict at the mine site later

lessons.heading: Good practice in the field
lessons.body: These are not statutory requirements, but they help you meet the 'fair opportunity' standard.
bullets: Use Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu or tok ples interpreters, and confirm people understand
Keep an attendance register with names, clans and villages
Make sure women, youth and absentee landholders' representatives are heard
Make audio recordings, with consent, and take written notes
Stay neutral. Do not promise outcomes, money or benefits
Write down every objection raised, even if it seems minor

keyPoints: Fair opportunity for the applicant, landholders and others affected
Confirm identity and affected status
The applicant explains the programme or proposals
Record AND assess the views of landholders
Adjourn by time or place, on conditions including costs
modules.tokPisin: Long hearing, Warden i mas givim gutpela taim long olgeta lain i gat wari long graun: ol papagraun, kampani na ol narapela. Warden i mas raitim na skelim tingting bilong ol.

quiz.prompt: Who must be given a fair opportunity to be heard at a Warden's hearing?
options: The applicant, landholders and other persons affected
quiz.explanation: Section 108 requires a fair opportunity for the applicant, the landholders and other persons affected by the proposal.

quiz.prompt: Why must the Warden confirm the identity of those present?
options: To confirm they are actually affected by the proposal
quiz.explanation: The Warden confirms identity and that each person is affected by the proposal, so the record shows who the real stakeholders are.

quiz.prompt: What must the Warden do with the views of landholders?
options: Ignore any view not submitted in writing
quiz.explanation: Section 108 requires the Warden to record AND assess the views of landholders and other affected persons.

quiz.prompt: Heavy rain stops most clan leaders from reaching the venue. What can the Warden do?
options: Proceed anyway, because the date is fixed
Adjourn the hearing to another time or place
quiz.explanation: The Warden may adjourn from time to time and from place to place, on conditions the Warden sets.

quiz.prompt: When adjourning, the Warden may set conditions that include…
quiz.explanation: Adjournment conditions may include conditions as to costs. Royalties and the grant itself are outside the Warden's role.

quiz.prompt: At the hearing, a landholder asks the Warden to guarantee a cash payment if they agree. The best response is…
options: Promise the payment to keep the peace
Stay neutral: explain the process and record the request
Tell them they have no rights
quiz.explanation: A Warden must stay neutral and cannot promise outcomes. Record the concern and explain how compensation is agreed or determined.

modules.title: The Warden's Report and Recommendation
modules.summary: Turning the hearing into a written report, and how the report feeds the Council's recommendation to the Minister.
objectives: State the deadline and recipient of the Warden's report
Describe what a good report contains
Explain how the report is used by the Mining Advisory Council
Know the Chief Warden's advisory role on EL extensions

lessons.heading: The reporting duty
lessons.body: Within 14 days after the hearing, the Warden must submit a written report on the hearing to the Executive Officer of the Board (now the Mining Advisory Council).
bullets: Deadline: 14 days after the hearing
Form: in writing
Recipient: the Executive Officer of the Board (Council)

lessons.heading: What a strong report contains
lessons.body: The Act sets the deadline and the recipient. Good practice sets the content. Your report is the Council's main evidence of what landholders think.
bullets: Application details: tenement type and number, applicant, area
Hearing details: dates, venues, adjournments and the reasons for them
Attendance: who attended, which clans and villages, and how identity was confirmed
The applicant's explanation of its programme or proposals
Landholder views, for and against, and any objections
Your assessment of those views, any land disputes, and compensation issues
Attachments: attendance register, copies of objections, photos and recordings

lessons.heading: From report to decision
lessons.body: The Council considers the Warden's report together with other required reports on the tenement, then makes its recommendation to the Minister.
bullets: A late, thin or inaccurate report can delay a decision or expose it to judicial review
Courts have examined whether the hearing and report steps were actually followed

lessons.heading: Chief Warden's advice on EL extensions
lessons.body: When deciding whether an exploration licence holder has paid the compensation it must pay, the Board relies on the advice of the Chief Warden. This is a specific Chief Warden function under s 16(3).

keyPoints: Written report within 14 days to the Executive Officer
The report is evidence. Make it complete, accurate and balanced.
The Council recommends to the Minister using the report
The Chief Warden advises the Board on EL compensation compliance
modules.tokPisin: Insait long 14 de bihain long hearing, Warden i mas raitim ripot na givim long Executive Officer bilong Mining Advisory Council.

quiz.prompt: Within how many days after the hearing must the Warden submit the report?
quiz.explanation: Section 109 requires a written report within 14 days after the hearing.

quiz.prompt: To whom is the Warden's report submitted?
options: The Executive Officer of the Board (Council)
quiz.explanation: The report goes to the Executive Officer of the Board, now the Mining Advisory Council.

quiz.prompt: What does the Mining Advisory Council do with the Warden's report?
options: Considers it with other reports and recommends to the Minister
Sends it to the National Court
Publishes it as the final decision
quiz.explanation: Under s 110, the Council considers the report with the other required reports and makes a recommendation to the Minister.

quiz.prompt: On an EL extension, whose advice does the Board rely on about whether compensation has been paid?
quiz.explanation: Section 28(4) says the Board relies on the advice of the Chief Warden on whether required compensation has been paid.

quiz.prompt: Which item is most important to include in a Warden's report?
options: The Warden's personal opinion of the company's share price
A record and assessment of landholder views and objections
quiz.explanation: The report must reflect the hearing. Its core content is the views of landholders and affected persons, and your assessment of them.

quiz.prompt: Why can a poor hearing or report be risky for the State?
options: It cannot. Reports are never checked.
The Minister's decision may be challenged and quashed in court
It automatically cancels all tenements in the province
It makes the Warden personally liable for royalties
quiz.explanation: The National Court has reviewed and quashed decisions where the required hearing and report steps were not properly followed.

modules.title: Compensation Principles and Agreements
modules.summary: The duty to compensate landholders, the rule against entry before compensation is settled, and the Chief Warden's review of compensation agreements.
objectives: Explain when a tenement holder must compensate landholders
State the rule on entering land before compensation is settled
Describe the Chief Warden's 14-day review of compensation agreements
Explain the legal effect of a registered agreement

lessons.heading: The duty to compensate
lessons.body: A tenement holder must compensate landholders for loss or damage caused by exercising rights under the tenement. The Act sets out the principles used to work out compensation. Wardens apply these principles when they determine disputes.
bullets: Typical heads of loss: deprivation of land use, damage to the land surface, crops, trees, improvements and other property
Compensation is for loss and damage. It is not payment for the minerals, which are regulated by the State.
lessons.note: Read the exact wording of the compensation principles in the current consolidated Act before determining any claim.

lessons.heading: No entry before compensation
lessons.body: The holder may not enter land for mining until a compensation agreement is registered, or compensation has been determined and paid or tendered.

lessons.heading: Review of compensation agreements
lessons.body: Proposed compensation agreements go to the Chief Warden. Within 14 days, the Chief Warden either states that he is willing to recommend registration, or asks for amendments.
bullets: Check the parties: are the right landholders and clans signing?
Check that the amounts and heads of loss are clear
Check that the terms are understood, and translated where needed

lessons.heading: Legal effect
lessons.body: Once registered, a compensation agreement is a condition of the tenement and a binding contract. A Warden's determination has the same effect. Breaching it puts the tenement at risk.

keyPoints: The holder compensates landholders for loss or damage
No entry for mining until an agreement is registered, or compensation is determined and paid or tendered
The Chief Warden reviews proposed agreements within 14 days
Registered agreements are tenement conditions and binding contracts
modules.tokPisin: Kampani i no ken go insait long graun long wok mining inap kompensesen agrimen i rejista pinis, o kompensesen i stret na ol i peim o ofaim pinis.

quiz.prompt: A tenement holder compensates landholders for…
options: The market value of the gold extracted
Loss or damage caused by exercising tenement rights
Nothing, because land is owned by the State
quiz.explanation: Compensation is for loss or damage caused by exercising rights under the tenement, such as loss of land use, crops, trees and improvements. It is not for the minerals.

quiz.prompt: When may a holder enter land to start mining?
options: As soon as the application is lodged
Once a compensation agreement is registered, or compensation is determined and paid or tendered
quiz.explanation: Entry for mining is barred until an agreement is registered, or compensation has been determined and paid or tendered.

quiz.prompt: How long does the Chief Warden have to respond to a proposed compensation agreement?
quiz.explanation: Within 14 days, the Chief Warden states willingness to recommend registration or requests amendments.

quiz.prompt: What are the Chief Warden's two possible responses to a proposed agreement?
options: Approve or send it to court
State willingness to recommend registration, or request amendments
Grant the tenement, or cancel it
quiz.explanation: The Chief Warden either indicates willingness to recommend registration or asks for amendments.

quiz.prompt: Once registered, a compensation agreement is…
options: A condition of the tenement and a binding contract
quiz.explanation: Registered agreements become conditions of the tenement and binding contracts.

quiz.prompt: Reviewing a draft agreement, you notice that one of the two landowning clans has not signed. What should you do?
options: Request amendments or clarification before recommending registration
Sign on behalf of the clan
quiz.explanation: Requesting amendments is exactly what the 14-day review is for. Make sure the right parties are bound before you recommend registration.

modules.title: Warden's Determination and Appeals
modules.summary: What happens when the holder and landholders cannot agree: the Warden hears the dispute, determines compensation, and either party may appeal.
objectives: Describe the steps in a Warden's compensation determination
Explain partial determinations
Explain how land disputes affect compensation
State the appeal route

lessons.heading: When there is no agreement
lessons.body: If the holder and the landholders cannot agree on compensation, either may ask for a determination. The Chief Warden fixes a place and date for the matter to be heard.
bullets: The Warden hears evidence and argument from both sides
The Warden applies the compensation principles of the Act
The Warden records the decision in writing
The Warden may decide part of a claim now and defer the rest

lessons.heading: Acting judicially
lessons.body: A determination affects legal rights, so the Warden must act fairly and impartially.
bullets: Give both sides notice and a chance to present evidence
Base the decision on the evidence and the statutory principles
Give written reasons that a court could follow on appeal
Declare any conflict of interest and step aside if one exists

lessons.heading: Land disputes
lessons.body: Where a land dispute makes agreement impracticable, for example two clans both claim the land, compensation is fixed through the Warden process and held in a statutory trust until the dispute is resolved. The project can continue lawfully while the rightful recipients are decided.

lessons.heading: Effect and appeal
lessons.body: A Warden's determination is a condition of the tenement and binding, like a registered agreement. A tenement holder or landholder dissatisfied with the determination may appeal to the National Court.

keyPoints: No agreement → the Chief Warden fixes a place and date → the Warden hears evidence and argument
Apply the statutory principles and give a written decision
Part of a claim may be decided now and the rest deferred
Disputed-land compensation is held in a statutory trust
Appeal lies to the National Court
modules.tokPisin: Sapos kampani na ol papagraun i no wanbel long kompensesen, Warden bai harim tok bilong tupela sait na mekim disisen. Husat i no amamas, em i ken apil long National Court.

quiz.prompt: If the parties cannot agree on compensation, who fixes the place and date for a determination?
quiz.explanation: The Chief Warden fixes the place and date, and the Warden then hears the matter.

quiz.prompt: In determining compensation, the Warden must…
options: Hear evidence and argument and apply the Act's principles
Split the difference between the two offers
quiz.explanation: The Warden hears evidence and argument, applies the statutory compensation principles and records a written decision.

quiz.prompt: Can a Warden decide only part of a compensation claim?
options: No, the whole claim must be decided at once
Yes, part can be decided and the rest deferred
Only if both parties sign a waiver
quiz.explanation: The Warden may determine part of a claim and defer the remainder.

quiz.prompt: Two clans claim the same land and cannot agree. What happens to the compensation?
options: It is paid to the larger clan
It is fixed through the Warden process and held in a statutory trust
quiz.explanation: Where a land dispute makes agreement impracticable, compensation is fixed through the Warden process and held in a statutory trust until the dispute is resolved.

quiz.prompt: A landholder is unhappy with the Warden's determination. Where can they appeal?
quiz.explanation: A dissatisfied tenement holder or landholder may appeal to the National Court.

quiz.prompt: The Warden assigned to a determination is related to one of the claimant clans. The best action is…
options: Hear it anyway, but be careful
Declare the conflict and ask the Chief Warden to reassign
Decide in favour of the other clan to look fair
Refuse to hear the matter at all
quiz.explanation: A determination must be impartial. Declare the conflict so that the Chief Warden can delegate the matter to another Warden.

modules.title: Enforcement, Protection and Accountability
modules.summary: The legal protections around the Warden's work: police help, offences for obstruction, immunity, and the regulations.
objectives: Know when police must assist a Warden
State the penalty for obstructing a Warden
Explain the Warden's immunity and its limits
Know where hearing procedures may be prescribed

lessons.heading: Police assistance
lessons.body: Police must assist a Warden or Department officer when required. A Warden can request police help where a hearing or site visit may be unsafe.
lessons.note: Plan ahead. Talk to the local police and District Administrator before hearings in areas with known tension.

lessons.heading: Offence of obstructing a Warden
lessons.body: Assaulting, hindering, obstructing or resisting a Warden is an offence under the unauthorised exploration provision.
bullets: Fine of up to K10,000, and/or
Imprisonment for up to four years

lessons.heading: Immunity
lessons.body: No liability attaches to a Warden acting in the exercise of his or her duties under the Act. This protects good-faith work. It does not cover acts outside the Warden's duties, such as accepting gifts or making side deals.

lessons.heading: Regulations and procedure
lessons.body: Regulations may prescribe the powers, functions and duties of Wardens and the practice and procedure of Warden's hearings. Read the Mining Regulation 1992 and MRA procedural notices, such as the Warden Hearing Requirement Notice, together with the Act.

lessons.heading: Integrity
lessons.body: Wardens hold public trust in communities where mining brings big money and strong emotions.
bullets: Never accept gifts, cash or favours from applicants or landholders
Record everything. A clear record protects you.
Report threats or bribery attempts to the Chief Warden immediately

keyPoints: Police must assist a Warden when required
Obstructing a Warden: up to K10,000 and/or 4 years
Immunity covers acts done in the exercise of Warden duties
Regulations may prescribe hearing practice and procedure
modules.tokPisin: Polis i mas helpim Warden taim em i askim. Sapos wanpela man i paitim o pasim rot bilong Warden, em i ken baim fain inap K10,000 o go long kalabus inap 4 yia.

quiz.prompt: When must police assist a Warden?
options: Never. Wardens rely on company security.
Only in the National Capital District
quiz.explanation: The Act requires police to assist a Warden or Department officer when required.

quiz.prompt: What is the maximum fine for assaulting or obstructing a Warden?
quiz.explanation: The maximum fine is K10,000, and/or imprisonment for up to four years.

quiz.prompt: What is the maximum prison term for obstructing a Warden?
quiz.explanation: Obstructing a Warden can lead to up to four years' imprisonment, and/or a fine of up to K10,000.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about a Warden's immunity is correct?
options: It covers anything the Warden does
It covers acts in the exercise of duties under the Act
quiz.explanation: No liability attaches to a Warden acting in the exercise of duties under the Act. Acts outside those duties are not protected.

quiz.prompt: Where can the practice and procedure of Warden's hearings be prescribed in more detail?
options: In regulations made under the Act
quiz.explanation: The regulation-making power allows regulations to prescribe Warden powers, functions and duties, and hearing practice and procedure.

quiz.prompt: After a hearing, an applicant's representative offers the Warden a 'thank you' envelope of cash. What should the Warden do?
options: Accept it, because the hearing is finished
Refuse it and report it to the Chief Warden
Accept it but declare it in the report
quiz.explanation: Accepting it would compromise impartiality and falls outside protected duties. Refuse it and report it.

modules.title: Field Practice: Case Scenarios
modules.summary: Apply everything you have learned to realistic situations a Warden faces in the field.
objectives: Apply the hearing, reporting and compensation rules to real situations
Choose lawful, fair and practical responses under pressure

lessons.heading: How to approach a scenario
lessons.body: For every field problem, ask yourself four questions.
bullets: 1. What does the Act require? (the statutory duty)
2. Who is affected, and have they had a fair opportunity to be heard?
3. What must I record?
4. Is this my decision, or the Chief Warden's, the Council's or the Minister's?

lessons.heading: The Warden's workflow at a glance
bullets: Application registered → Registrar confers with the Chief Warden (7 days)
Objection period (at least 30 days) → hearing 7 to 14 days later
Hearing under s 108: identify people, applicant explains, record and assess views, adjourn if needed
Report under s 109 to the Executive Officer within 14 days
Council recommends (s 110) → Minister decides
Compensation: agreement reviewed by the Chief Warden (14 days), or a Warden's determination → appeal to the National Court
lessons.body: Keep this sequence in mind. Most mistakes happen when a step is skipped.

keyPoints: Duty → fairness → record → whose decision
When in doubt: adjourn, record and refer to the Chief Warden
modules.tokPisin: Taim yu stap long fil, tingim: Act i tok wanem? Husat i gat wari? Mi mas raitim wanem? Disisen em bilong husat?

quiz.prompt: You arrive at the hearing venue and the applicant's representatives have not turned up. What is the best option?
options: Hear only the landholders, then recommend refusal
Adjourn on conditions, which may include costs against the applicant
Cancel the application on the spot
Hold the hearing by phone with no landholders present
quiz.explanation: The applicant must be able to explain its proposals. Adjourning on conditions, including costs, protects fairness for everyone.

quiz.prompt: It is day 16 after the hearing and your report is not finished. Which duty have you already breached?
options: None, because there is no deadline
quiz.explanation: Section 109 requires the written report within 14 days after the hearing.

quiz.prompt: A company starts clearing land before any compensation agreement is registered or compensation determined. This is…
options: Allowed once the tenement application is lodged
Contrary to the rule against entry before compensation is settled
Only a problem on State land
quiz.explanation: Entry for mining is barred until an agreement is registered, or compensation is determined and paid or tendered.

quiz.prompt: During a hearing, a person says they are a landholder, but nobody present recognises them. You should…
options: Record their claim and note that their identity and affected status could not be confirmed
Treat them as the main landholder
quiz.explanation: Section 108 requires the Warden to confirm identity and affected status. Recording the claim with that note keeps the record accurate and fair.

quiz.prompt: Landholders demand that the Warden approve the tenement at the end of the hearing. The correct explanation is…
options: The Warden approves it on the spot
The Warden reports, the Council recommends and the Minister decides
The Registrar decides the next day
quiz.explanation: The Warden's role is to hear and report. The grant decision follows the Council's recommendation to the Minister.

quiz.prompt: A crowd becomes aggressive and threatens the Warden during a hearing. Which statements are correct?
options: Nothing can be done because the hearing must continue
The Warden may adjourn, police must assist when required, and obstructing a Warden is an offence
The Warden must pay compensation to calm the crowd
quiz.explanation: Safety comes first. Adjourn, call on police assistance, and remember that obstructing a Warden is an offence.

glossary.definition: A lease for small-scale mining of alluvial deposits, often taken up by landholders.
The person or company applying for a tenement or for an extension of one.
The senior Warden appointed under s 16. Performs Warden duties plus specific functions such as scheduling hearings, reviewing compensation agreements and advising the Council.
An agreement between a tenement holder and landholders on compensation. Once registered, it is a tenement condition and a binding contract.
A written instrument by which the Chief Warden passes powers to a Warden (s 16(4)). The power to delegate cannot itself be delegated.
A Warden's written decision fixing compensation when the parties cannot agree. It may be appealed to the National Court.
The officer of the Board (Mining Advisory Council) who receives objections and Warden's reports.
A tenement that authorises searching for minerals in a defined area.
A Warden's hearing conducted under s 108, where the applicant explains its proposal and affected people are heard.
A person who owns or holds an interest in land, including customary landowners.
A lease for land used for activities that support mining, such as camps, plant and storage.
Formerly the Mining Advisory Board. It considers Warden's reports and other reports and recommends to the Minister.
A tenement for access infrastructure such as roads, pipelines, power lines and tailings lines.
A tenement that authorises medium-scale mining.
Mineral Resources Authority, the body that administers the Mining Act. Its Managing Director appoints Wardens.
A written objection to an application, lodged by any person with the Registrar before the deadline (s 107).
The officer who registers applications, fixes hearing dates with the Chief Warden and publicises applications (ss 105–106).
A tenement for large-scale mining projects, usually linked to a mining development contract.
A trust in which compensation is held where a land dispute makes agreement impracticable.
The general term for an EL, ML, SML, AML, LMP or Mining Easement granted under the Act.
A statutory office holder appointed under s 16 whose functions, powers and duties are set out in the Act.
